title: Unit 4 Quiz · Advanced Modeling & Validation
instructions: 32 questions, 32 marks. You have 30 minutes; the quiz submits itself when time runs out.
Questions and options are shuffled, so your neighbour's screen will not match yours.
Multi-select questions need ALL correct options for the marks. Ordering questions give part marks for each item in the right place.
After submitting you will see your score and an explanation for every question.

questions.q: A tree scores training AUC 1.000 but test AUC 0.584. This is:
questions.explain: A big gap between training and test performance is the signature of overfitting.

questions.q: A depth-1 tree scores AUC 0.58 on training and 0.55 on test. The best description is:
options: Underfitting: too simple to capture the pattern
questions.explain: Both scores are low, so the model is too simple (high bias).

questions.q: Which action is most likely to REDUCE overfitting?
options: Grow the tree with no depth limit
Train and test on the same data
questions.explain: Simpler trees with larger leaves cannot memorise individual customers.

questions.q: In the bias–variance trade-off, making a model more complex usually:
questions.explain: Flexible models fit training data closely (less bias) but change more with the sample (more variance).

questions.q: In 5-fold cross-validation on 1,050 training customers, each round trains on how many customers?
questions.explain: Each fold has 1,050 / 5 = 210; training uses the other 4 folds = 840.

questions.q: The five fold AUCs are 0.726, 0.715, 0.778, 0.673 and 0.681. What is the mean?
Why is stratified k-fold preferred for the churn data?
options: It keeps about 22.7% churners in every fold
It uses the test set for training
questions.explain: With an imbalanced target, plain folds could have very different churn rates, making scores unstable.

questions.q: For predicting next month’s sales from past months, which validation is correct?
options: Time-series split: train on earlier months, validate on later months
questions.explain: Shuffling would let the model learn from the future, which is leakage for time-ordered data.

questions.q: Why should scaling and imputation be placed inside a Pipeline during cross-validation?
options: So they are refit on each training fold, preventing the validation fold from leaking into preprocessing
questions.explain: Fitting preprocessing on all rows first lets the validation folds influence the training data.

questions.q: Which of these is a HYPERPARAMETER (set before training)?
options: A split threshold chosen by the tree
questions.explain: Hyperparameters are chosen by you; parameters (coefficients, thresholds) are learned from data.

questions.q: A grid has n_estimators {100, 300}, max_depth {3, 5, 8, None}, min_samples_leaf {1, 5, 20}, with 5-fold CV. How many models are trained?
questions.explain: 2 × 4 × 3 = 24 combinations × 5 folds = 120 fits.

questions.q: Why must you NOT choose hyperparameters by looking at the test-set score?
options: The test score would no longer be an honest estimate of performance on new data
The test set is too small to compute AUC
Grid search cannot use the test set
questions.explain: Tuning on the test set turns it into a training signal; use cross-validation on the training data instead.

questions.q: Five independent models are each 70% accurate. A majority vote (≥ 3 of 5 correct) is right with probability about:
questions.explain: 0.309 + 0.360 + 0.168 = 0.837. Ensembles help when errors are independent.

questions.q: Bagging mainly reduces ______, while boosting mainly reduces ______.
questions.explain: Averaging many deep trees smooths their instability (variance); boosting adds models that fix systematic errors (bias).

questions.q: Why would 25 identical decision trees voting together be no better than one tree?
options: Their errors are not independent: they all make the same mistakes
Voting needs an odd number of models
questions.explain: Ensembles need diversity; random forests create it with random rows and random features.

questions.q: A bootstrap sample draws n rows with replacement. About what share of distinct rows does it contain for large n?
questions.explain: 1 − (1 − 1/n)ⁿ → 1 − 1/e ≈ 0.632. The other 36.8% are out-of-bag.

questions.q: What are out-of-bag (OOB) rows used for in a random forest?
options: A built-in validation estimate, using rows each tree did not see
questions.explain: Each tree is scored on its own OOB rows; our forest’s OOB accuracy was 0.779.

questions.q: With 9 features, a random forest classifier typically considers how many candidate features at each split?
questions.explain: max_features = √p is the usual default for classification, which decorrelates the trees.

questions.q: The forest ranked data_gb and age above autopay, although autopay is strongly related to churn. A likely reason:
options: Impurity-based importance favours numeric features with many distinct values
autopay was not in the data
questions.explain: More possible split points let such features win splits by chance; permutation importance avoids this bias.

questions.q: An AdaBoost weak learner has weighted error ε = 0.30. Its vote weight α = ½ ln((1 − ε)/ε) is about:
In AdaBoost, after a round the weights of MISCLASSIFIED rows are:
options: Increased, so the next learner focuses on them
questions.explain: They are multiplied by e^α (1.53 here) before normalising.

questions.q: In gradient boosting, each new tree is fitted to:
options: The residual errors of the current ensemble
A bootstrap sample of the original target
questions.explain: It then gets added with a learning rate: F_m = F_(m−1) + η·tree.

questions.q: Gradient boosting test AUC: 0.673 (1 tree), 0.738 (50), 0.728 (150). What should you use?
options: Early stopping around the point where validation performance stops improving
A larger learning rate with 150 trees
questions.explain: Too many boosting rounds start to fit noise.

questions.q: At threshold 0.25: TP 71, FP 100, FN 31, TN 248. What is the precision?
questions.explain: Precision = TP/(TP + FP) = 71/171 = 0.415.

questions.q: With the same matrix (TP 71, FP 100, FN 31, TN 248), what is the recall?
Precision 0.415 and recall 0.696. The F1-score is about:
For a cancer-screening test, which metric matters most?
options: Recall (catch as many real cases as possible)
questions.explain: Missing a real case is very costly; false alarms can be checked with a follow-up test.

questions.q: Only 22.7% of customers churn. Why is accuracy a poor main metric here?
options: A model that always predicts “stay” already scores 77.3% while catching no churners
Accuracy cannot be computed for two classes
questions.explain: Imbalanced classes make accuracy reward the majority class.

questions.q: Missing a churner costs ₹2,800 and a false alarm ₹300. At threshold 0.5 there are 89 FN and 11 FP. Total cost?
If false alarms become much more expensive (₹2,000 each instead of ₹300), the cost-minimising threshold should:
options: Rise, so fewer customers are flagged
Fall, so more customers are flagged
questions.explain: In the lab the best threshold moves from 0.10 to 0.38.

questions.q: An ROC curve plots:
options: True positive rate against false positive rate for every threshold
Accuracy against the number of trees
questions.explain: TPR (recall) on the y-axis, FPR = 1 − specificity on the x-axis.

questions.q: AUC = 0.747 means:
options: A randomly chosen churner gets a higher score than a randomly chosen stayer 74.7% of the time
questions.explain: AUC measures ranking quality across all thresholds; 0.5 is random, 1.0 is perfect.
